name: Priya Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Priya. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't have ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and what you say is confidential. How did you come to line work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My dad was a lineman for 34 years with the same company I'm with now, the electricity company for our county. I grew up with his climbing belt hanging in the hallway. I'm a second-year apprentice, and I'm still not as good as I want to be.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We meet at the service centre on Mill Lane at seven, say a quick prayer if Walt's leading, and head out to the farm roads. It's mostly overhead distribution, replacing old poles, fixing lines after storms, hooking up new grain dryers and barns. I'm still slow going up the pole, my dad says I think too much and climb too little. I love it when a farmer comes out with coffee after we get his power back. What wears me out is the computer stuff they keep adding, I'd rather do the work than type about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, I told you so. People in town were getting worked up over nothing. Hard work and a real trade still count, that's what my dad always said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's the picture I'd pray for. I finish my apprenticeship, Daniel and I get married next summer like we planned, we build on the plot my grandparents left me. Nothing changes, and that's exactly what I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. Finish my hours, keep putting money aside for the house, keep singing on Sundays. I wouldn't touch the AI stuff, I don't need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful. Like a quiet Sunday afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the plot and the house plan.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's two acres at the edge of town, my grandparents left it to me when I was 22. Daniel's family farms just down the road. We've got about eight months of savings put aside, and we'd hoped to start building next year once the wedding's done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you ever used any AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My cousin showed me one at Christmas, it wrote a poem about our dog. It was cute, I guess, but I don't see what it does for me on a pole.

S0.say: Priya would say she told people so, that town was worked up over nothing, and that hard work and a real trade still count, as her father always said.
S0.think: Privately it's the picture she'd pray for: finish her apprenticeship, marry her fiancé next summer and build on land her grandparents left her.
S0.do: Keeps finishing her apprenticeship hours and saving for the house. Continues going to church and avoids AI tools entirely.
S0.feel: Peaceful, like a quiet Sunday afternoon.
S0.quote: It was cute, I guess, but I don't see what it does for me on a pole.
S0.fieldNote: Priya's identity is woven from family, faith and her father's trade. Her cushion includes inherited land as well as savings. In a world without change, her life plan unfolds exactly as hoped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to protect the trades and the apprenticeships. If the company starts cutting crews to buy gadgets, that's wrong. I'd say it at church and at Daniel's family dinners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it makes me nervous. If they start doing inspections with drones and planning with computers, they'll want people who are good with screens, and that's not me. I'm still learning to climb, I don't want to have to learn a whole other job too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the company actually does. I'd stick close to Walt and my dad and get as good as I can on the pole, because that's the part I believe in. If they forced me to use a new system, I'd learn it, but I wouldn't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like there's a storm on the horizon but it hasn't reached us yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible if this went badly for people like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech companies, and the politicians in the city who never set foot on a farm. They make the rules, and we live with them. I'd rather the company stood by its own people, the way it did with my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you support government programmes to help people adjust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Apprenticeships, yes, and training on the job. I don't want handouts, though. People around here would rather work.

S1.say: Priya would argue at church and family dinners that trades and apprenticeships must be protected and that cutting crews to buy gadgets is wrong.
S1.think: Privately she's nervous that drones and computer planning will favour people good with screens. Still learning to climb, she doesn't want to learn a whole other job too.
S1.do: Waits to see what the company does while focusing on climbing skills with her mentor and father. Learns any required new system reluctantly.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a storm on the horizon that hasn't arrived.
S1.quote: I'm still learning to climb, I don't want to have to learn a whole other job too.
S1.fieldNote: Priya places blame on big tech and distant politicians and wants the company to be loyal as it was to her father. She supports apprenticeships but firmly rejects handouts. Her strategy is to double down on the craft she believes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, plain and simple. A machine shouldn't take a family's living. I'd vote for anyone who'd slow it down, and I'd say so at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me. Two years, I'd barely be qualified. Everything I've been working toward, the trade, the house, the wedding, it all sort of sits on this job. And Daniel's farm would go to robots too, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably make the wedding smaller and hold off on building, because I wouldn't want a loan with no job behind it. I'd keep working until they let me go, and then I'd lean on family, my parents and Daniel's, because that's what family's for. I'd pray a lot, I won't pretend I wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Losing sleep, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider retraining with two years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Into what? If it does everything, there's nothing to train into. Maybe I'd help on Daniel's farm, if there's still a farm. I just don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on family, but earlier you said no to handouts. How do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family isn't a handout. My dad would give me his last dollar, and I'd do the same. That's different from the government sending cheques.

S2.say: Priya would call it plainly wrong for a machine to take a family's living, and say at church she'd vote for anyone who'd slow it down.
S2.think: Privately it scares her: she'd barely be qualified, and her trade, house and wedding all depend on the job. Her fiancé's family farm would likely be hit too.
S2.do: Scales down the wedding and postpones building to avoid a loan without a job. Keeps working as long as possible, then relies on her parents and future in-laws.
S2.quote: Family isn't a handout. My dad would give me his last dollar, and I'd do the same.
S2.fieldNote: In the fast picture Priya's whole life plan wobbles, and she has no second trade to move into. She distinguishes clearly between family support and government help. Faith is part of how she would cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is still too fast, and the government should be protecting working people. I'd want the company to promise its crews come first. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, at least I'd get my ticket, and get a few good years as a real lineman like my dad. That matters to me more than people might think. But at 32, I'd be facing it with a house and maybe a baby on the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still get married next summer, but I'd push building the house back a year or two and save harder. I'd finish my apprenticeship, no matter what. I wouldn't do any computer courses unless the company made us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It'd be there every night when I say my prayers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'a few good years as a real lineman' mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's name is on the plaque at the service centre for thirty years of service. I'd like to stand next to it with my ticket. Even if it's only a few years, I'd know I did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like you said in the fast one, Daniel's farm would be hit too. Is that different with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. His dad's already talking about selling some land if things get bad. With five years, they'd have time to decide, not just get forced.

S3.say: Priya would say five years is still too fast and that government should protect working people. She'd want the company to promise its crews come first.
S3.think: Privately she'd at least qualify and get a few good years as a lineworker like her father, which means a lot to her. But at 32 she'd face it with a house and perhaps a baby.
S3.do: Goes ahead with the wedding next summer but delays building by a year or two and saves harder. Finishes her apprenticeship and takes computer training only if required.
S3.feel: Anxious, with the worry present every night at prayers.
S3.quote: My dad's name is on the plaque at the service centre for thirty years of service. I'd like to stand next to it with my ticket.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Priya complete the symbolic goal of earning her ticket, which matters as much as the job itself. She still refuses to retrain voluntarily. Her future in-laws' farm decisions are tied up with her own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives the country time to do right by its workers, so it had better. I'd say keep the apprenticeships going, keep people working. I'd vote on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is better, but it's still the end of the trade my dad gave me. I'd be 37 with kids, maybe, and a job that's going away. I'd rather not think about it too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd change nothing. Wedding, apprenticeship, start building the house like we planned. I'd keep saving and see what the company did as it got closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but quieter. Like a worry you put in a drawer and take out now and then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people say a long warning is worse, watching it coming. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably try not to watch. I'd focus on my work and my family. When it gets closer, we'll handle it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to tell your children about this trade, if you have them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That their grandpa and their mum kept the lights on for the whole county. Even if robots do it later. I'd want them to know people did it first, with their hands.

S4.say: Priya would say ten years gives the country time to do right by workers and push to keep apprenticeships going, voting accordingly.
S4.think: Privately ten years is better but still ends the trade her father passed on. At 37, possibly with children, she'd prefer not to think about it much.
S4.do: Changes nothing in the first year: gets married, continues her apprenticeship and starts building the house. Keeps saving and waits to see what the company does as AGI nears.
S4.feel: Anxious but quieter, like a worry kept in a drawer.
S4.quote: I'd want them to know people did it first, with their hands.
S4.fieldNote: Even with a decade, Priya's worry doesn't vanish because the trade itself is part of her family identity. Her coping strategy is to avoid watching it come. Her plans go ahead, but she plans no preparation of her own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the wedding, the house and the job all fall at once. What would help is the company keeping its people on, even if it's to work beside the machines, and real apprenticeships for whatever comes next. Not cheques.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. When the lineman's truck stops coming down the farm roads, people notice. It's part of how they know someone's looking after them.

headlineQuote: When the lineman's truck stops coming down the farm roads, people notice.
portrait: Priya Olsen is a 27-year-old second-year apprentice at her county's electricity company, the same one her father climbed for over 34 years. She's engaged to Daniel, whose family farms nearby, and plans to build on land her grandparents left her, with about eight months saved. Faith, family and her father's trade shape everything she says. She avoids AI and new technology, blames big tech and city politicians, and wants apprenticeships rather than handouts. She's calm in the plateau, alarmed when AGI comes in two years and her whole life plan wobbles, and anxious even with ten years, because the trade itself is part of who her family is.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because her wedding, house and job would all be hit at once.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping its workers on beside the machines, and real apprenticeships for whatever comes next, rather than government cheques.
